children: Rising bets on another US rate hike pushed the yen back towards 160 per dollar and Japan's 10-year bond yield towards 2.9% on November 13, testing Tokyo's tolerance.

The dollar climbed above JPY160 in New York trading on November 12, the yen's weakest level since September, and touched about JPY160.02 in Tokyo the next day before settling near JPY159.97 in mid-afternoon,
News On Japan
reported. The benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) yield rose about seven basis points to around 2.87% at the day's high, while the US 10-year traded near 5.13%, according to
investingLive
As a result, Japan is being squeezed from both sides.

A cheaper yen raises the bill for an economy that imports almost all of its energy, at a time when the Iran war is keeping crude near $96 a barrel. Yet defending the currency with higher interest rates raises the cost of carrying gross public debt that the IMF put at about 214% of GDP in 2024. As a result, markets are probing whether JPY160, the level that drew joint US-Japanese action in the summer, is still Tokyo's line.
Washington's money behind the line

Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on November 13 that she was seeing one-sided, rapid currency moves and would stay in contact with the US Treasury to respond appropriately. She added that the two governments had set out a shared stance on exchange rates at their summit, and declined to comment on intervention. Atsushi Mimura, the vice finance minister for international affairs, had warned a day earlier that it was too early to forget the summer's operation.

That operation was large. Japan spent JPY15.4 trillion ($96.44bn) buying yen on July 30, July 31 and August 3, including JPY5.55 trillion on July 31, according to quarterly intervention data the finance ministry published on November 9.

The New York Fed then disclosed on November 12 that the US Treasury had bought yen in the third quarter, its first yen purchase since 1998. It spent about JPY79bn of euros from its Exchange Stabilisation Fund on July 31, a token sum next to Tokyo's but a clear signal of political backing for the Japanese government. The dollar subsequently fell from about JPY164 to about JPY155 over those few days.

The US moves were not unexpected, however, as Tokyo had been lining up US support since May. The joint action in July then bought a little over three months before the yen drifted back to where it started.
A rate gap that keeps reopening

The pressure starts in Washington. The Federal Reserve raised rates in September to a range of 3.75% to 4%, then held on October 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voting for another quarter-point rise. US core consumer prices rose 0.3% m/m in October, above forecasts of 0.2%. New York Fed President John Williams meanwhile said inflation was still too high and the Fed had more work to do, and markets now price a high probability of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December 9 decision.

The Bank of Japan, for its part, has been moving in the same direction, only from a much lower base. It lifted its policy rate to 1.25% in September, then held it on October 30 by an 8-1 vote, with board member Hajime Takata arguing for 1.5%.
Most economists polled by
Reuters

now expect a move to 1.5% at the December 17-18 meeting. If the Fed also moves, the gap between the two policy rates stays above 2.5 percentage points, and it is that gap that keeps the yen under pressure.
Policy rates of the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan at end-month, %. Source: Bank for International Settlements via IntelliNews Lambda.
Imported inflation, imported fiscal pain

The weak yen is passing straight into prices. Import prices measured in yen rose 24.5% y/y in September, down only slightly from a peak of 30.4% in June, Bank of Japan data show. Corporate goods prices were also up and rose 6.8% y/y, while core consumer inflation climbed to 2.1% in September, back above 2% for the first time in nine months.
Japan's import price index in yen terms, % y/y. Source: Bank of Japan via IntelliNews Lambda.

Each attempt to cushion households only adds to the borrowing bill. The Japanese cabinet released JPY616bn of emergency reserve funds for fuel subsidies as recently as September, and Katayama said on November 13 that winter subsidies for utility bills would be paid early from reserve funds. A cut in the consumption tax on food to 1% from 8% takes effect in April 2027 for a maximum of two years, and ministries have already asked for a record JPY143 trillion for the next fiscal year.

Bond investors have noticed these moves. The 10-year yield touched 3% on September 1 for the first time since 1996, and the 20-year stood at 3.726% on November 13. Nine of Japan's 10 largest life insurers expect long-term rates of 3% or more by the end of March 2027, which would push refinancing costs higher across a debt stock that is rolled over constantly.
Yen per US dollar, monthly average. Source: Bank for International Settlements via IntelliNews Lambda.
Testing the line

The next fortnight will prove crucial as it sees the release of Japan's preliminary 3Q26 GDP figures on November 16 and more US price data, before the Fed and the Bank of Japan meet in December. Analysts at Mizuho Securities now expect the dollar to keep rising against the yen on a resilient US economy and sticky inflation,
investingLive

reported. Intervention can slow that move, but it cannot close the rate gap, and every trillion yen spent defending the currency is drawn from reserves that Tokyo also needs as its buffer against the bond market.

This pattern this year has seen Tokyo warning of speculation in March, the yen jumping to 155 on suspected intervention in May, then the cost of the defence began to show up in Japan's Treasury holdings by June, and Fed tightening has since left the Philippines and other Asian bond markets exposed as well.
What has changed this autumn is that the Fed is raising rates again, which makes the 160 line more expensive to hold than it was in the spring.

title: Japan faces currency hell as yen plunges and bond yields explode
